name: Airbyte
license: Elastic License 2.0 (source-available, not OSI open source): the platform since 0.30.0 (September 2021), every connector since July 2025; the Airbyte Protocol, Python CDK and `abctl` are MIT; Airbyte Cloud is proprietary
summary: An ELT platform you can host yourself: hundreds of connectors, each a Docker image speaking one JSON protocol, scheduled by services on Kubernetes.
intro: Airbyte has two halves. The platform is a set of services on Kubernetes: an API server and web UI, a Postgres database that keeps connection settings and job history, Temporal for scheduling, and workers that start each sync as its own pods. Connectors are Docker images that follow the Airbyte Protocol. A source answers `spec`, `check`, `discover` (list the tables or API resources it can read) and `read`, which streams records plus `STATE` messages; a destination’s `write` loads them. The platform saves the last state, so the next sync only reads what changed, and Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server and MongoDB sources can follow the database log (CDC). Most connectors no longer need code: 514 of the 690 in the main repo are “manifest-only”, a YAML file run by a shared image, which is what the no-code Connector Builder writes.

You can run it yourself with the Helm chart on an existing cluster, or with `abctl`, which creates a one-node kind cluster inside Docker. Airbyte Cloud bills in credits: on Standard ($20 a month with 5 credits, then $5 per credit) a million API rows costs 6 credits and a GB from a database or file costs 4, so roughly $30 and $20. Plus sells prepaid packages from $189 a month for 40 credits. Pro and Enterprise Flex are priced by capacity, in “Data Workers” that each run about three syncs at once, through sales. PyAirbyte runs the same connectors inside a Python process and caches the rows in a local DuckDB file by default.
strengths: A large catalogue: about 600 sources and 80 destinations in the main repo, with CDC for the main databases
Connector Builder: point-and-click REST API sources whose YAML manifest you can export and edit
The same connectors run self-hosted, in Airbyte Cloud and from Python with PyAirbyte
A language-neutral protocol: any program in a Docker image that reads config and prints JSON can be a connector
Self-hosted use is free, with no limits on volume, users or connections
limits: Not OSI open source: ELv2 forbids selling Airbyte as a hosted service, and since July 2025 that covers every connector too
Heavy to self-host: even a laptop install runs Kubernetes (kind), Temporal, Postgres and MinIO; Docker Compose installs were deprecated in 1.0 (2024)
Cloud meters database and file sources by the size of the serialized records, which Airbyte says is likely larger than in your database; overage is billed in arrears and syncs keep running
Batch only: the fastest Cloud schedule is 1 hour on Standard, 15 minutes on Plus, 5 minutes on Pro
Self-hosted releases slowed after 2.0 (October 2025): 2.1 came in April 2026 marked experimental, and Self-Managed Enterprise users are told not to upgrade but to move to Cloud

sections.title: Which part is under which licence

items.name: Platform
items.text: Moved from MIT to the Elastic License 2.0 with version 0.30.0 on 27 September 2021. Free to run, change and use internally; not to resell as a hosted ELT service.

items.name: Connectors
items.text: About two dozen “strategic” connectors (Postgres, MySQL, Salesforce, Snowflake and others) moved to ELv2 in June 2023; a July 2025 change moved the rest. Earlier contributions keep their original licence.

items.name: Protocol, Python CDK and `abctl`
items.text: The message format, the Python connector development kit and the local installer remain MIT, so you can build your own connectors under any licence.

items.name: Airbyte Cloud, Enterprise
items.text: Hosted and enterprise editions need a commercial agreement with Airbyte.

story: Michel Tricot had run integrations at LiveRamp, where his team built thousands of connectors; John Lafleur had founded Anaxi. Interviewing data teams in 2020, they found that every company “had to develop connectors internally, even though they were paying for another product”: hosted tools covered popular sources but not the long tail, and could not be changed. Their answer was an open-source platform where anyone could add a connector.

They started in July 2020 and tagged the first alpha that September, with three sources and two destinations. The community grew it fast: in 2022 about 70% of new connectors came from outside contributors. A $26M Series A in 2021 was followed that December by $150M from Altimeter and Coatue at a $1.5 billion valuation. Airbyte Cloud launched in April 2022, the same month Airbyte bought Grouparoo, an open-source reverse-ETL tool.

To stop larger companies reselling the project as a service, Airbyte moved the platform from MIT to the Elastic License in September 2021, then its key connectors in 2023 and the rest in 2025. Version 1.0 in September 2024 swapped Docker Compose for Kubernetes everywhere, with `abctl` for single machines.

choices.choice: Connectors as Docker images speaking a JSON protocol
choices.why: Contributors could write a connector in any language and test it alone, and the platform could run, isolate and upgrade each one the same way.

choices.choice: Declarative YAML connectors and a no-code builder
choices.why: Most REST APIs differ only in authentication, pagination and record paths. Describing those in a manifest made hundreds of API connectors cheaper to build and maintain than Python code.

choices.choice: The Elastic License instead of MIT
choices.why: Airbyte wanted to keep self-hosting free while preventing cloud providers and competitors from selling the same software as a managed service.
